passage_text: Researchers at the University of Greenfield examined the impact of a novel cognitive training program on working memory in adults aged 25–45. Sixty participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group (no training), Group A (30‑minute training sessions twice weekly), Group B (45‑minute sessions twice weekly), and Group C (30‑minute sessions three times weekly). Baseline working‑memory scores were obtained using the Digit Span task. After 12 weeks, post‑intervention scores were recorded. Table 1 summarizes the mean scores and changes for each group. The data suggest that longer sessions (Group B) may be associated with greater improvement, whereas adding a third weekly session (Group C) gave no gain over Group A. The researchers plan to conduct a follow‑up study to explore the underlying neural mechanisms using fMRI. The current findings provide preliminary evidence that structured, moderate‑intensity training can enhance working memory, though the optimal dosage remains unclear. Future analyses will examine dose–response relationships and potential moderators.
stem: Which group showed the largest absolute improvement in working‑memory score?
explanation: Group B increased from 47 to 62, a change of 15 points, which is the greatest among all groups.
trap: Option D incorrectly assumes Group C had the largest change.

stem: What is the unweighted mean of the four group changes in Table 1?
explanation: Correct: (2 + 10 + 15 + 10) / 4 = 37 / 4 = 9.25 points. Why the others are wrong: A) 8.5 results from mis-adding the changes. C) 10 is the change in Groups A and C, not the mean of all four. D) 11 overstates the sum of the changes divided by four.
trap: Mis-adding the four changes or dropping the control group's change of 2 from the average gives a wrong mean.

stem: Which statement is best supported by Table 1?

options.A: The training had no effect on working memory.
options.B: The control group improved more than the training groups.
options.C: Group B improved by 13 points more than the control group.
options.D: The variability within groups is negligible.

explanation: Correct: Group B changed by 15 points and the control group by 2, a difference of 13 points. Why the others are wrong: A) every training group improved by 10 to 15 points versus 2 for control. B) the control group improved by only 2 points, the least of any group. D) the table gives no measure of variability, so nothing can be said about it.
trap: Inferring that variability is small or that an effect size is large when the table reports only group means and no spread.

stem: Which pair of groups differs in session duration while holding session frequency constant (twice weekly)?
explanation: Correct: Group A (30 min) and Group B (45 min) both train twice weekly, so only duration differs. Why the others are wrong: A) control receives no training, so this compares training itself, not duration. C) Group A and Group C both use 30-minute sessions; they differ in frequency, not duration. D) Group B and Group C differ in both duration and frequency, so neither is held constant.
trap: Choosing Group B versus Group C because their gains differ, without noticing that both session length and frequency differ.
